description: Table 4 is a single rendered table (no plots or micrographs) reporting Vickers hardness (HV) of 19Al alloys as a function of aging treatment. Columns are: "Vickers hardness (HV)", "Solution-treated", and aging times "1 h", "3 h", "6 h", "10 h". Rows are aging temperatures: "525 °C aging", "550 °C aging", "575 °C aging", "600 °C aging", "625 °C aging", "650 °C aging". The "Solution-treated" value, 263.8 ± 1.1 HV, is given once in a cell spanning all six temperature rows, so it applies to every aging temperature. Each aging cell gives mean ± standard deviation. Reading the grid: at 525 °C hardness rises only slightly from 562.3 ± 8.9 HV (1 h) to 614.4 ± 17.3 HV (10 h). At 550 °C it rises to 778.5 ± 23.7 HV at 6 h then falls to 735.5 ± 23.5 HV at 10 h. At 575 °C hardness is 458.7 ± 11.5 HV at 1 h, peaks at 904.5 ± 12.0 HV at 3 h, then decreases to 835.4 ± 30.9 HV (6 h) and 843.7 ± 7.9 HV (10 h). At 600 °C the values are uniformly high and almost flat: 901.2 ± 14.6, 899.8 ± 6.8, 895.3 ± 16.2 and 917.8 ± 24.5 HV. At 625 °C they are ~855-871 HV and at 650 °C ~801-811 HV, both essentially time-independent. The table therefore demonstrates that aging temperature, not aging time, dominates the hardness of these 19Al alloys, with the highest values around 900 HV reached at 600 °C; all aged values are much harder than the solution-treated 263.8 HV.

observations.observation: The table lists Vickers hardness (HV) for six aging temperatures: 525 °C, 550 °C, 575 °C, 600 °C, 625 °C and 650 °C aging.
The four aging durations tested are 1 h, 3 h, 6 h and 10 h.
A single solution-treated hardness of 263.8 ± 1.1 HV is printed in one cell spanning all six aging-temperature rows, i.e. it applies to every aging condition.
Every aged condition is substantially harder than the solution-treated state: the lowest aged value is 458.7 ± 11.5 HV (575 °C, 1 h) versus 263.8 ± 1.1 HV solution-treated.
At 525 °C aging hardness increases monotonically with time from 562.3 ± 8.9 HV (1 h) to 614.4 ± 17.3 HV (10 h).
At 550 °C aging hardness peaks at 6 h with 778.5 ± 23.7 HV and then drops to 735.5 ± 23.5 HV at 10 h.
At 575 °C aging hardness is lowest at 1 h (458.7 ± 11.5 HV), peaks at 3 h with 904.5 ± 12.0 HV, then falls to 835.4 ± 30.9 HV (6 h) and 843.7 ± 7.9 HV (10 h).
At 600 °C aging hardness is high and nearly time-independent: 901.2 ± 14.6 HV (1 h), 899.8 ± 6.8 HV (3 h), 895.3 ± 16.2 HV (6 h) and 917.8 ± 24.5 HV (10 h).
The 600 °C, 10 h condition gives the highest value in the table, 917.8 ± 24.5 HV.
At 625 °C aging the values stay between 855.6 ± 20.8 HV (1 h) and 870.7 ± 16.1 HV (6 h) with little time dependence.
At 650 °C aging the values are the lowest of the aged group and nearly constant, ranging only from 801.5 ± 20.3 HV (3 h) to 811.2 ± 19.5 HV (10 h).
All entries are reported as mean ± standard deviation in HV, as indicated by the ± symbol in every cell.
The caption states that the table gives Vickers hardness values of the 19Al alloys after different aging treatments.

subfigures.description: Single table of Vickers hardness (HV) for 19Al alloys: six aging temperatures (525-650 °C) against four aging times (1, 3, 6, 10 h), plus a common solution-treated value of 263.8 ± 1.1 HV spanning all rows. Values are means ± standard deviation.
